---
title: "Traits in Rust"
---

A **trait** describes behavior that many types can share: "any type that implements this trait can do these things." If you know C# interfaces, Dart abstract classes, or Python `Protocol`s, you already have most of the idea. Rust then adds a few abilities those languages don't have.

This completes the picture from the first lesson:

```
   ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌────────────────────────┐
   │ struct/enum  │     │ impl Type    │     │ impl Trait for Type    │
   │   (data)     │  +  │ (its own     │  +  │ (shared behavior       │
   │              │     │  methods)    │     │  contract)             │
   └──────────────┘     └──────────────┘     └────────────────────────┘
     WHAT it is          WHAT it can do        WHAT it has in common
                                               with other types
```

---

## 1. Defining and implementing a trait

```rust
trait Shape {
    fn area(&self) -> f64;                 // required: implementors must write it
    fn name(&self) -> String {             // default: implementors may override it
        String::from("unknown shape")
    }
}
```

```rust
struct Circle { radius: f64 }
struct Rect   { w: f64, h: f64 }

impl Shape for Circle {
    fn area(&self) -> f64 { std::f64::consts::PI * self.radius.powi(2) }
    fn name(&self) -> String { "circle".into() }   // overrides the default
}

impl Shape for Rect {
    fn area(&self) -> f64 { self.w * self.h }      // keeps the default name()
}
```

Note that the trait implementation is a **separate block** from the type definition. You can add a trait to a type long after the type was written, even in a different file or module. In C#, a class has to list its interfaces when it is declared.

Default methods can call required methods. This is how a small trait can provide a lot of functionality:

```rust
trait Shape {
    fn area(&self) -> f64;
    fn is_large(&self) -> bool { self.area() > 100.0 }  // built on area()
}
```

---

## 2. Using traits: writing code for "any type that…"

There are three common ways to write it. They mean the same thing here:

```rust
// 1. impl Trait in argument position: the shortest form
fn print_area(s: &impl Shape) {
    println!("area = {:.2}", s.area());
}

// 2. Generic with a trait bound: the full form
fn print_area<T: Shape>(s: &T) { /* ... */ }

// 3. where clause: easier to read when there are many bounds
fn print_area<T>(s: &T) where T: Shape { /* ... */ }
```

You can combine bounds with `+`:

```rust
fn report<T: Shape + std::fmt::Debug>(s: &T) {
    println!("{:?} has area {}", s, s.area());
}
```

A practical generic function:

```rust
fn largest<T: PartialOrd>(items: &[T]) -> Option<&T> {
    let mut best = items.first()?;        // `?` on Option: return None if empty
    for item in items {
        if item > best { best = item; }   // `>` works because T: PartialOrd
    }
    Some(best)
}
```

Without `T: PartialOrd`, the compiler rejects `item > best`. It won't assume that an arbitrary `T` can be compared. **The trait bound is the permission.**

---

## 3. Static vs dynamic dispatch

This is the most important design decision with traits. Rust lets **you** choose how a trait method call is resolved.

**Static dispatch (generics, `impl Trait`).** The compiler generates a separate copy of the function for each concrete type you use. This is called *monomorphization*:

```
  Source code:                       What the compiler generates:
  ┌──────────────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ fn print_area<T: Shape>  │  ──►  │ fn print_area_Circle(&Circle)│
  │     (s: &T)              │       │ fn print_area_Rect(&Rect)    │
  └──────────────────────────┘       └──────────────────────────────┘
  ✅ Zero runtime cost, calls can be inlined
  ⚠️ Larger binary; one call can only hold ONE concrete type
```

**Dynamic dispatch (`dyn Trait`).** The concrete type is decided at runtime through a lookup table, like virtual methods in C#:

```rust
let shapes: Vec<Box<dyn Shape>> = vec![
    Box::new(Circle { radius: 1.0 }),
    Box::new(Rect { w: 2.0, h: 3.0 }),
];                                       // mixed types in one Vec ✅

let total: f64 = shapes.iter().map(|s| s.area()).sum();
```

A `&dyn Shape` or `Box<dyn Shape>` is a **fat pointer**, made of two pointers:

```
  Box<dyn Shape>
 ┌──────────────┬──────────────┐
 │ data ptr ────┼──┐           │
 │ vtable ptr ──┼──┼─────┐     │
 └──────────────┴──┼─────┼─────┘
                   ▼     ▼
           ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────────────────────┐
  heap:    │ Circle   │ │ vtable for Circle:       │
           │ radius:1 │ │  area → Circle::area     │
           └──────────┘ │  name → Circle::name     │
                        │  drop, size, align       │
                        └──────────────────────────┘
```

```
┌───────────────────┬───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┐
│                   │ Generics / impl Trait     │ dyn Trait                  │
├───────────────────┼───────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┤
│ Resolved          │ compile time              │ runtime (vtable)           │
│ Speed             │ fastest (inlinable)       │ small indirection cost     │
│ Mixed collections │ ❌                        │ ✅ Vec<Box<dyn Shape>>     │
│ Binary size       │ grows per type            │ one copy                   │
│ Default choice?   │ ✅ yes                    │ when heterogeneity needed  │
└───────────────────┴───────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────┘
```

Not every trait can be used as `dyn`. A trait is **dyn-compatible** (formerly called "object safe") only if its methods don't, for example, return `Self` or have their own generic type parameters. The vtable needs a fixed set of concrete functions, and those features would prevent that.

You can also return a trait from a function:

```rust
fn make_shape() -> impl Shape { Circle { radius: 2.0 } }  // one hidden concrete type

fn pick(big: bool) -> Box<dyn Shape> {                     // can differ at runtime
    if big { Box::new(Rect { w: 9.0, h: 9.0 }) } else { Box::new(Circle { radius: 1.0 }) }
}
```

---

## 4. Associated types

Some traits need a type as a placeholder inside them. The best-known example is `Iterator`:

```rust
struct Countdown(u32);

impl Iterator for Countdown {
    type Item = u32;                          // associated type: "I yield u32s"
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u32> {
        if self.0 == 0 { return None; }
        self.0 -= 1;
        Some(self.0 + 1)
    }
}
```

You write only `next()`. In return you get **dozens of default methods** for free (`map`, `filter`, `sum`, `collect`, `zip`, …):

```rust
let total: u32 = Countdown(3).map(|x| x * 10).sum();   // 30 + 20 + 10 = 60
```

**When to use an associated type and when to use a generic parameter:**

```
  trait Iterator { type Item; }   → each type has ONE natural Item
                                     (a Countdown can't yield both u32 and String)

  trait From<T> { ... }           → a type can implement it MANY times
                                     (String: From<&str>, From<char>, From<Box<str>> ...)
```

---

## 5. Standard library traits you'll use constantly

Many Rust features are just traits. Implement the trait, and the feature works for your type:

```
┌─────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
│ Trait           │ Unlocks                        │ Usually...               │
├─────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
│ Debug           │ {:?} printing                  │ #[derive]                │
│ Display         │ {} printing, .to_string()      │ manual impl              │
│ Clone / Copy    │ .clone() / implicit copying    │ #[derive]                │
│ PartialEq / Eq  │ == and !=                      │ #[derive]                │
│ PartialOrd / Ord│ < > and .sort()                │ #[derive] or manual      │
│ Hash            │ use as HashMap key             │ #[derive]                │
│ Default         │ T::default()                   │ #[derive] or manual      │
│ From / Into     │ type conversions, `?` errors   │ manual impl              │
│ Iterator        │ for loops, .map(), .filter()   │ manual impl              │
│ Add, Mul, ...   │ + * operators                  │ manual impl              │
│ Drop            │ cleanup code (destructor)      │ manual impl (rarely)     │
└─────────────────┴────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┘
```

**`Display`: user-facing formatting**

```rust
use std::fmt;

struct Point { x: i32, y: i32 }

impl fmt::Display for Point {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
        write!(f, "({}, {})", self.x, self.y)
    }
}
// println!("{}", Point { x: 1, y: 2 });  → (1, 2)
```

**`From`: conversions (and you get `Into` for free)**

```rust
struct Celsius(f64);
struct Fahrenheit(f64);

impl From<Celsius> for Fahrenheit {
    fn from(c: Celsius) -> Self { Fahrenheit(c.0 * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0) }
}

let f: Fahrenheit = Celsius(100.0).into();   // `.into()` works automatically
```

`From` is also what lets the `?` operator from the enums lesson convert error types automatically.

**Operator overloading is just a trait**

```rust
use std::ops::Add;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
struct Vec2 { x: f64, y: f64 }

impl Add for Vec2 {
    type Output = Vec2;
    fn add(self, o: Vec2) -> Vec2 { Vec2 { x: self.x + o.x, y: self.y + o.y } }
}
// let c = a + b;   ✅
```

---

## 6. More powerful features

**Supertraits: "to implement A, you must also implement B"**

```rust
trait Describe: std::fmt::Display {          // Describe requires Display
    fn describe(&self) -> String {
        format!("<<{}>>", self)              // allowed: self is guaranteed Display
    }
}
```

This looks like inheritance, but it is only a **requirement**, not inheritance. No fields or implementations are passed down.

**Blanket implementations: implementing a trait for every type that meets a condition**

This is how `Into` comes for free in the standard library:

```rust
impl<T, U> Into<U> for T where U: From<T> {
    fn into(self) -> U { U::from(self) }
}
// "For EVERY T, if U can be built From<T>, then T is Into<U>."
```

You can write your own. For example, `impl<T: Display> Describe for T {}` gives `describe()` to every printable type at once.

**The orphan rule (coherence)**

```
  You may write  `impl Trait for Type`  only if Trait OR Type is defined in your crate.

  impl Shape   for Circle    ✅ both yours
  impl Display for Circle    ✅ the type is yours
  impl Shape   for Vec<i32>  ✅ the trait is yours
  impl Display for Vec<i32>  ❌ neither is yours (std owns both)
```

This rule stops two libraries from defining conflicting implementations. The usual workaround is the **newtype pattern** from the structs lesson: `struct MyList(Vec<i32>);`, then implement `Display` for `MyList`.

---

## 7. Traits vs enums: choosing your polymorphism

Now that you know both, you can make a real architectural choice. Both of these model "a shape that has an area":

```
  ENUM (closed set)                        TRAIT (open set)
  enum Shape { Circle{..}, Rect{..} }      trait Shape { fn area(&self) -> f64; }

  ✅ match is exhaustive                   ✅ anyone (other crates, plugins)
  ✅ easy to add new OPERATIONS               can add new TYPES
     (just write another fn with match)    ✅ easy to add new types
  ❌ adding a VARIANT means updating       ❌ adding a new METHOD means
     every match                              updating every impl
  ✅ no heap / vtable needed               ⚠️ dyn requires Box/& + vtable

  Use when: you own and know every case    Use when: the set of types must stay
  (states, messages, AST nodes)            open (plugins, library extension points)
```

This trade-off is known as the **expression problem**. Rust gives you both tools, so choose based on which axis, operations or types, you expect to grow.

## Comparison with languages you know

```
┌─────────────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┬────────────┬───────────────┐
│ Feature             │ Rust trait   │ C# interface │ Dart       │ Python        │
│                     │              │              │ abstract   │ Protocol/ABC  │
├─────────────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┼────────────┼───────────────┤
│ Default methods     │ ✅           │ ✅ (C# 8+)   │ ✅         │ ✅            │
│ Impl for existing   │ ✅           │ ❌ (only ext │ ❌ (only   │ ❌            │
│ (foreign) types     │              │  methods)    │  extension)│               │
│ Static dispatch     │ ✅ default   │ partial      │ ❌         │ ❌            │
│ Associated types    │ ✅           │ ❌           │ ❌         │ ❌            │
│ Blanket impls       │ ✅           │ ❌           │ ❌         │ ❌            │
│ Operator overload   │ via traits   │ operator kw  │ operator kw│ __dunder__    │
│ Fields / state      │ ❌ never     │ ❌           │ ✅         │ ✅            │
└─────────────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┴────────────┴───────────────┘
```

---

### Key takeaways
1. A trait is a **behavior contract**, implemented in a separate `impl Trait for Type` block. It can be added to existing types.
2. **Default methods** let a small trait provide a lot of functionality (see `Iterator`).
3. **Generics / `impl Trait`** give static dispatch with zero cost and are the default. **`dyn Trait`** gives runtime polymorphism through a vtable.
4. Many language features (`==`, `+`, `{}`, `for`, `?`) are **powered by traits**.
5. Rust has **no inheritance**. You build designs from structs, enums, and traits, and you choose between enums (closed set) and traits (open set) on purpose.

You now have Rust's three building blocks: **structs, enums, and traits**. Good next topics are **ownership and borrowing in depth** (the thing that makes Rust unique), **generics and lifetimes** (expanding on the trait bounds above), or **iterators and closures** (where traits show up most in daily code).
